questions.explanation: The prompt is assembled first, counted with the invoked model's own tokenizer, checked against the window, then the output budget is set by subtraction before the call, and the stop reason confirms nothing was truncated unexpectedly.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: Place the parts of a prompt in the order AWS's guidance says they should appear in the request.
options: The instruction or question
Role and background context
Worked examples
Reference data or documents
questions.explanation: AWS advises giving the background and the data first, showing worked examples before the query, and placing the instruction at the end so the most relevant tokens sit closest to where generation starts.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: Match each prompt construct to what it does.
options: The task and rules the model must follow
Background or data the model reads before answering
What must be kept out of the output
Reusable prompt text with variable placeholders
questions.explanation: The exam guide names context, instruction and negative prompts as prompt constructs: context supplies the material to work on, the instruction states the task, a negative prompt excludes outputs, and a template adds reusable placeholders.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: Match each prompt-engineering risk to the mitigation that addresses it.
options: Keep secrets out of the prompt entirely
Use Guardrails prompt-attack and content filters
Constrain the assistant's instructions and tool access
Curate and vet data sources before any training job
questions.explanation: Each risk has its own control: exposure is prevented by keeping sensitive content out of prompts, poisoning by vetting training data, hijacking by limiting what the assistant may do, and jailbreaking by Guardrails filters that block the bypass attempt and the prohibited output.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: A planner must answer a complex scheduling question, a single wrong answer is unacceptable, and the budget allows several generations per request. Which prompt technique fits?
options: Add three to five worked examples that demonstrate the output format
Run one chain-of-thought generation and keep the first answer
Ask for the answer in a single sentence to save tokens
Sample several reasoning paths and keep the answer that appears most often
questions.explanation: Self-consistency samples several reasoning paths and keeps the majority answer, trading extra generations for a higher chance of correctness. Examples and a single reasoning run do not produce a majority vote.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: A summarizer for a simple, well-specified task ships this week, no vetted examples exist yet, and the token and latency budget is tight. Which prompting approach fits the first release?
options: Five-shot prompting with five checked examples
Self-consistency over five generations of the same prompt
Prompt chaining that splits the work across three calls
Zero-shot prompting: an instruction with no examples
questions.explanation: With a simple, well-specified task and no examples available, an instruction-only prompt is the documented fit and the cheapest option. Examples, repeated sampling and chaining all add tokens and latency for a task that does not need them.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: Match each prompt-engineering practice to the failure it is meant to prevent.
prompts: Test every prompt revision against a fixed set of representative inputs
Keep a held-out set of prompts that the team never tunes against
Keep the task instruction short and unambiguous
Pin each approved prompt as a version before it reaches production
options: Production wording that nobody can trace or roll back
A revision that quietly breaks prompts the team had already validated
The model choosing between two plausible readings of the task
Gains that come mostly from tuning against the prompts used to measure them
questions.explanation: Testing against a fixed set catches regressions, a held-out set keeps the measurement honest, concise instructions remove ambiguity, and versioning makes every change traceable and reversible. Each practice closes a different way a prompt release can fail.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: A marketing team generates product scenes with an image model on Amazon Bedrock. The prompt describes the scene in detail, yet the results keep drifting away from it. Which control makes the output follow the written prompt more strictly?
options: Lower cfgScale so the model has more freedom around the description
Fix the seed to one value and keep it on every request
Raise cfgScale, which tightens adherence to the written prompt
Increase numberOfImages so more candidates come back
questions.explanation: cfgScale sets how strictly a generated image follows the written prompt, so raising it tightens adherence and lowering it gives the model more freedom. A fixed seed only makes separate runs comparable to each other, and returning more images does not change how closely any one image follows the text.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: A support assistant must refuse every request for account credentials, and the rule has to apply on every turn without being retyped. In a Converse API request, where do these standing instructions belong?
options: Repeat the rule at the end of every user message so the model sees it again
Add it to additionalModelRequestFields, which is passed through to the model
Send it as a message with a system role inside the messages array
Put it in the top-level system field, which applies to the whole request
questions.explanation: Standing instructions belong in the top-level system field, which Converse applies to the whole request alongside the messages array rather than inside it. Repeating the rule in user text wastes tokens and invites injection, additionalModelRequestFields carries model-specific parameters, and Converse messages hold user and assistant turns only.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: A knowledge base call fails with a message saying the augmented prompt exceeds the model's character limit. Which response matches the documented remediations?
options: Raise numberOfResults so the model receives more context to work with
Lower numberOfResults and shorten the prompt template or the user query
Raise maxTokens so the model can finish the answer it has already started
Re-embed the corpus with a larger embedding model and run the call again
questions.explanation: AWS documents exactly three fixes for an oversized augmented prompt: lower numberOfResults, re-create the data source with smaller chunks, or shorten the prompt template or the user query. Raising numberOfResults adds passages and makes the prompt larger, while maxTokens governs output length rather than the size of the incoming prompt.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: A network operations group wants the model to narrate each troubleshooting step before it commits to a root cause, and nobody in the group has written down an example of a correct diagnosis to place in the prompt. Which approach fits?
options: Three or four completed incident write-ups attached to the prompt as demonstrations
One hand-written diagnosis supplied as the single demonstration
A reasoning cue that asks the model to work through the fault first, with no demonstrated pair anywhere in the prompt
Several linked calls, each taking the result of the previous call as its input
questions.explanation: Zero-shot chain-of-thought uses a reasoning cue with no worked example, which matches a team that wants step-by-step troubleshooting but has no sample diagnosis to offer. Few-shot prompting would fit only if the group had checked examples to attach, and prompt chaining reorganizes the work instead of making one pass explain itself.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: A team is editing the prompt template that a knowledge base uses when it generates answers. Which statements about that template are correct?
options: numberOfResults controls how many passages fill that placeholder
The template selects the chunks itself, so editing it changes what gets retrieved
The template must contain the placeholder that carries retrieved passages, or the model never sees them
The passage placeholder is optional, because retrieval results reach the model automatically
Dropping the placeholder for output format instructions removes citations from the answer
The template does not decide which chunks are retrieved; retrieval settings do that
questions.explanation: AWS requires the passages placeholder in a generation prompt, ties its size to numberOfResults, and warns that dropping the output-format placeholder silently removes citations from the answer. Which chunks arrive is decided by retrieval configuration rather than by the template text, and passages never reach the model without their placeholder.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: Match each image-generation control to the job it performs.
prompts: Choose between standard and premium image fidelity
Ask for several variations of the same scene in one request
Guide style and composition with up to five extra source images
Pin the run so comparable requests start from the same noise
options: seed
reference images
quality
numberOfImages
questions.explanation: Fidelity is the quality control, which Amazon Nova Canvas exposes as standard or premium, numberOfImages sets how many images a single request returns, reference images supply up to five extra pictures that guide style and composition, and a fixed seed lets comparable runs start from the same noise so results can be compared.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: In AWS's own worked example an instruction costs 80 tokens and one labeled example costs 60 tokens. What does a prompt with five examples cost relative to the zero-shot instruction alone?
options: 1.75 times the zero-shot input tokens
3.25 times the zero-shot input tokens
1.46 times the zero-shot input tokens
4.75 times the zero-shot input tokens
questions.explanation: The zero-shot prompt is 80 tokens, so five examples give 80 plus 5 times 60, which is 380 tokens, or 4.75 times the zero-shot input for the same single answer. Three examples would cost 260 tokens or 3.25 times, one example 140 tokens or 1.75 times, and 1.46 is the ratio of five shots to three shots rather than to zero-shot. That multiplier is why AWS calls three to five examples the sweet spot for simple classification.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: A team estimates input sizes before calling an embedding model because counting every prompt would cost another API call. Which pair of conversion rules matches what AWS publishes?
options: About 4 characters per token for every model, as third-party calculators assume
About 6 characters per token for embeddings and about 4.7 characters per token for quotas
About 6 characters per token for customization quotas and about 4.7 characters per token for English embeddings
One token equals one English word, so word counts can stand in for token counts
questions.explanation: AWS publishes roughly 6 characters per token for fine-tuning quota and dataset planning in the Prepare model customizations documentation, and roughly 4.7 characters per token for English sent to Titan Text Embeddings V2, where 8,192 tokens is about 38,502 characters. The popular 4-characters-per-token rule is a third-party number AWS never published, the two AWS rules are not interchangeable, and tokenization splits words, so word count is not token count.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: A team runs a reasoning prompt on Titan Text Premier. Longer derivations cut off before the final steps are written, and the team refuses to shorten the reasoning. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Lower temperature so the model reaches the answer in fewer steps
Raise maxTokenCount toward the model's output maximum so the derivation can finish
Trim the system prompt so more input tokens fit in the context window
Enable streaming so tokens reach the interface while the model is still generating
questions.explanation: The cut-off is an output-length limit: chain-of-thought moves cost to the output side, where the Titan Text default maxTokenCount of 512 bites first, so raising maxTokenCount, up to 3,072 on Premier, lets the derivation finish. Lower temperature only changes sampling, trimming the system prompt frees input space the request never lacked, and streaming changes when tokens arrive rather than how many may be generated.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: A team is enabling Amazon Bedrock's chain-of-thought feature for a support assistant. Which statements about the feature are correct?
options: AWS describes it as giving the model a chance to think before it responds, which can often improve accuracy
It adds latency and increases the number of output tokens each request produces
AWS states that simple tasks are not good candidates for it
It requires three to five worked examples in the prompt before it can function
In the Bedrock console the feature is presented under the name model reasoning
It removes the need to evaluate prompts because the reasoning is now explicit
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock documents the feature as model reasoning in the console and says it can often improve model accuracy by giving the model a chance to think before it responds, with increased latency and increased output tokens as the explicit cost; AWS also states that simple tasks are not good candidates. A reasoning cue works without any worked example, and explicit reasoning does not replace evaluating the prompt on a held-out set.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: Place the steps AWS's prompt-engineering decision path follows when choosing a technique for a new task, in order.
options: Evaluate the prompt on a held-out set of prompts the team has not tuned against
Ask whether the task is simple and well specified
Add examples only when three to five good ones exist, with the instruction at the end
Add a reasoning cue when the task needs multi-step reasoning or maths
Sample several reasoning paths and keep the majority answer when one wrong answer is unacceptable
Fine-tune the model before trying any prompt change
questions.explanation: The decision path opens with whether the task is simple and well specified, moves to few-shot examples only when three to five good ones exist with the instruction at the end, adds chain-of-thought for multi-step reasoning or maths, applies self-consistency only when a single wrong answer is unacceptable, and finishes with evaluation on a held-out prompt set before anything ships. Fine-tuning is a later rung of the customization ladder, not the first move.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 - Choose effective prompt engineering techniques
questions.question: Match each prompt-engineering technique to the situation AWS's guidance recommends it for.
options: Format or tone control: 3 to 5 examples, instruction last
Simple, well-specified task: instruction only, least format control
Decomposable work: step N output becomes step N plus 1 input
Multi-step reasoning or maths: better accuracy, higher cost
High-stakes reasoning: sample paths and keep the majority
questions.explanation: AWS pairs each technique with its situation: a simple, well-specified task takes an instruction alone, format or tone control takes three to five examples with the instruction at the end, reasoning tasks take chain-of-thought at the cost of latency and output tokens, high-stakes answers take self-consistency over several sampled paths, and decomposable work takes chaining where one call's output feeds the next.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A legal technology company wants a model to absorb the vocabulary, citation style, and conventions of contract language across a large corpus of unlabeled contracts before any task-specific training. Which approach matches this goal?
options: Instruction tuning on a small set of annotated contract questions
Retrieval-augmented generation over an index of the same contracts
Reinforcement fine-tuning with a reward model that scores citation quality
Continuous pre-training on the contract corpus to adapt the model to the domain
questions.explanation: Continuous pre-training, also called domain adaptation, feeds unlabeled domain text into the model so it absorbs the field's vocabulary and style. Instruction tuning needs labeled pairs, retrieval-augmented generation injects documents at query time without changing weights, and reinforcement fine-tuning optimizes against a reward signal.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: An ML engineer is assembling the dataset for a supervised fine-tuning job that will route support tickets to the right team. Which property of the dataset matters most for the job to succeed?
options: Curated, labeled examples that represent the range of real tickets, including difficult cases
The largest possible volume of unlabeled text, regardless of where it came from
Examples drawn only from tickets the current system already handles correctly
Records assembled without licensing or privacy review so the job can start sooner
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning quality depends on curated, representative, labeled examples, with governance over licensing and privacy applied before training. Volume alone does not help, a set of easy cases leaves failure modes untrained, and skipping review creates compliance risk rather than speed.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Place the steps of preparing a dataset for a fine-tuning job in the order they occur.
options: Format the approved records into the training file schema and upload them to the location the job will read
Define the target behavior and the examples that count as a correct response
Curate the collected records: remove duplicates, correct errors, strip personal data, and confirm licensing
Run the fine-tuning job and compare the result against a held-out validation set
Sample production inputs so the examples cover real requests, including edge cases
questions.explanation: Target behavior is defined first, then representative data is sampled, then curation and data governance are applied, then the curated records are formatted and uploaded, and only then does the job run with evaluation on held-out data.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Match each fine-tuning approach to the description of what it does.
options: Human reviewers rank candidate outputs and a reward model is learned from those rankings
Training on instruction and response pairs so the model learns to follow directions reliably
Reusing knowledge the model already has from one task when adapting it to a related task
Feeding large volumes of unlabeled domain text so the model absorbs the field's vocabulary and style
questions.explanation: Instruction tuning trains on instruction and response pairs, continuous pre-training feeds unlabeled domain text, transfer learning reuses knowledge from a related task, and RLHF learns a reward model from human rankings of candidate outputs.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: During a supervised fine-tuning job, training loss keeps falling while loss on the held-out set falls and then rises. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The job is underfitting, so it needs more epochs
The model is overfitting, so an earlier checkpoint or more varied examples should be used
The validation set leaked into training, so the test file must be removed from Amazon S3
The learning rate is too low, so it should be raised sharply
questions.explanation: Rising validation loss while training loss falls is the signature of overfitting. Stopping at an earlier checkpoint or adding more varied examples addresses it.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Place the steps of a managed supervised fine-tuning project in the order they occur.
options: Evaluate the custom model against a held-out set the job never saw
Curate and format labeled examples, then store the training file in Amazon S3
Deploy the custom model with the capacity option the workload needs and point the application at it
Create the customization job with the chosen base model and hyperparameters
Monitor job status and training metrics until the job completes
questions.explanation: A supervised fine-tuning job starts with curated labeled data, then trains, then is evaluated on held-out data before deployment. Evaluation before deployment is what prevents shipping a model that only memorized the training set.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Match each training concept to the description that fits it.
options: Data withheld from training to detect overfitting
One complete pass over the training dataset
Number of examples processed before one weight update
Loss of broader skills after narrow fine-tuning
Size of each weight update step during training
questions.explanation: An epoch is one pass over the data, learning rate sets the update step size, batch size sets how many examples precede an update, and a held-out set detects overfitting. Catastrophic forgetting is the loss of broader skills after narrow fine-tuning.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A company runs a high-volume intent-classification workload on a large foundation model. Accuracy is good, but per-request cost and latency are too high, and the company can generate unlimited labeled outputs from the current model. Which approach best reduces cost while preserving the current behavior?
options: Train a smaller student model on outputs generated by the large model
Continue pre-training the large model on more unlabeled text
Deploy a pre-trained model from SageMaker JumpStart and use it as-is
Add the full label taxonomy to every prompt as context
questions.explanation: Distillation trains a smaller student on a teacher's outputs, which fits a team that can generate training data at scale from a strong model; the other options leave the large model in the serving path or change the behavior rather than preserve it.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A team fine-tunes a model on thousands of pairs in which a task instruction is followed by a high-quality response, so the model will follow new instructions reliably at inference time. Which method is being used?
options: Reinforcement learning from human feedback
Instruction tuning
Transfer learning from an unrelated task
Continuous pre-training on domain text
questions.explanation: Instruction tuning is supervised training on instruction-response pairs that teaches a model to follow directions, whereas RLHF trains on human preference rankings and continuous pre-training consumes unlabeled domain text.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: After fine-tuning a general assistant on 800 refund-policy tickets only, the team finds that it answers refund questions well but has become unreliable on unrelated general requests. What is the most likely cause?
options: Underfitting, because the model never learned the refund policy
Data leakage, because the validation records were contaminated
Catastrophic forgetting, because narrow tuning overwrote broader behavior
Overfitting, because validation loss rose during training
questions.explanation: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when fine-tuning on a narrow dataset overwrites general capabilities, and the usual remedy is to blend broader instruction data with the narrow examples or reduce the tuning intensity.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A team monitors a fine-tuning job and sees training loss and validation loss both staying high and moving together. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Overfitting, because the model has memorized the training records
Data leakage, because the validation records were seen during training
The model has converged and is ready to deploy
Underfitting, because the model is not capturing the pattern in the data
questions.explanation: Loss that stays high and nearly identical on both splits is the signature of underfitting, which calls for a richer model, more data or less regularization; overfitting instead shows falling training loss against rising validation loss.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A team reports 99 percent accuracy for its fine-tuned support model, but the evaluation prompt-response pairs were included in the training file. How should the team produce a trustworthy result?
options: Rebuild the evaluation set from records that were never used in training
Add the same records to the validation file so both sets match
Train for more epochs so the model generalizes to those records
Publish the number with a note that the model is highly confident
questions.explanation: An evaluation set must be held out from fine-tuning data, otherwise the score measures memorization rather than generalization; the fix is a validation file excluded from training and referenced separately in the job configuration.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A compliance team must answer questions from policy documents that are revised weekly, and answers must reflect the newest revision without any retraining. Which approach best fits?
options: Fine-tune the model on each weekly revision of the documents
Run continuous pre-training on the weekly document drops
Ground the model with retrieval over the current documents
Distill the model so the policy text is stored in its weights
questions.explanation: Frequently changing, citable facts are the classic case for retrieval-augmented generation rather than training, because the index can be refreshed without a job; fine-tuning and continuous pre-training would lag behind the weekly revisions.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Which practices are necessary for a fine-tuning dataset that will produce a reliable model?
options: Put the evaluation prompts into training to avoid wasting records
Deduplicate the file before reporting how many records you have
Relax the label guidelines so more annotators can contribute quickly
Hold out a validation file that training never sees
Pad the dataset with unrelated web text to reach the size quota
Sample production traffic to confirm the examples look like real requests
questions.explanation: Curation, a held-out validation split and representativeness against production inputs are all named in objective 3.3's data-preparation list, while leaking evaluation data, inconsistent labels and off-domain padding all degrade the result.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Which statements about reinforcement learning from human feedback are correct?
options: It needs no training because the prompt alone changes the behavior
Humans rank or choose preferred model outputs
It aligns behavior with preferences rather than teaching new facts
A model-as-judge can supply the reward signal in reinforcement fine-tuning
It removes the need for any held-out evaluation set
questions.explanation: RLHF trains on human preference rankings to align behavior, and AWS's reinforcement fine-tuning accepts rule-based or model-as-judge rewards as an automated version of the same idea; it is a training method and does not replace evaluation.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Place the customization approaches in the order of increasing commitment described by AWS's customization ladder.
options: Fine-tuning on labeled examples
Using the model as-is
Retrieval-augmented generation
Continued pre-training on a large domain corpus
Prompt engineering
questions.explanation: AWS's ladder runs from using the model as-is through prompt engineering and retrieval to fine-tuning and finally continued pre-training, so each step commits more data, cost and irreversibility than the one before it.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Match each fine-tuning data concern to what it requires.
options: Consistent, accurate targets produced by annotators
Controls for access, licensing and PII in the data
Human preference rankings used as a training signal
Removing irrelevant, low-quality and duplicate records
Input variety that matches what production will send
questions.explanation: These are five of the six data-preparation items named in objective 3.3 (curation, governance, size, labeling, representativeness and RLHF), and each one guards a different way the dataset can fail the model.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Match each training data requirement to what it describes.
prompts: Messages array with user and assistant turns
Record longer than the model's token cap
options: Where the job reads the training file from
Layout for non-conversational records
Layout for conversational records
A record that must be split into smaller pieces
The JSONL file format Bedrock requires
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock reads .jsonl files in which each line is one record, uses prompt and completion for non-conversational data and a messages array for conversations, points at the file through trainingDataConfig.s3Uri, and rejects records that exceed the model's token limit.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A support assistant must reply in a fixed house style. The team has hundreds of accepted replies, the style guide rarely changes, and stuffing the guide plus worked examples into every request has already made latency and token cost unacceptable. Which approach fits next?
options: Distill the current assistant into a smaller student model trained on its outputs
Fine-tune a copy of the model on the accepted replies so the style becomes the default
Add the full style guide and several worked examples to every request
Run continuous pre-training on the company's public marketing pages
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning teaches the behavior from accepted examples so the style no longer has to ride in every request. Distillation needs a teacher that already performs the task, continuous pre-training needs a large unlabeled corpus, and adding the guide to each request is the approach that already failed.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A team is considering fine-tuning a foundation model for document question answering. Which statements about that choice are correct?
options: It needs labeled examples of the task, not only raw documents
It removes the need to hold out an evaluation set
Fresh facts need another training run, so weekly changes lag behind
It is AWS's recommended first step for document question answering
Answers cannot cite the source document the way retrieval can
It is available for every model in the Bedrock catalog
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning changes weights, so it cannot point at sources, lags behind changing documents and depends on labeled pairs, while AWS positions retrieval as the starting point for document question answering. Customization is not offered for every model and never replaces a held-out evaluation set.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Match each training signal to the customization technique that learns from it.
prompts: Teacher-model responses generated automatically from a prompt set
Scores produced by an automatic reward function for each response
Instruction and response pairs written for one fixed task
Large volumes of unlabeled text from the target domain
Documents retrieved at query time and placed in the prompt
options: Retrieval grounding, which changes no weights at all
Model distillation, which trains a smaller student model
Continued pre-training, which absorbs the domain's vocabulary and style
Supervised fine-tuning, which teaches the model to follow the task
Reinforcement fine-tuning, which optimizes against the reward signal
questions.explanation: Each technique consumes a different signal: teacher outputs, an automatic reward, labeled pairs, raw domain text, or no training signal at all when documents are supplied at query time. Picking the wrong signal is the most common customization mistake.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A team is moving a fine-tuning job onto multiple GPUs. The model weights do not fit in a single GPU's memory, while the training dataset itself is modest. Which strategy fits?
options: Model parallelism, which partitions the model across the GPUs
Data parallelism, which keeps a full model replica on each GPU
Both equally, because the choice depends only on dataset size
Neither; the job should stay on one GPU and stream data from Amazon S3
questions.explanation: Model parallelism partitions the model itself across devices and is the documented answer when the model will not fit in one GPU's memory. Data parallelism is the mirror case, where the model fits on one device and the dataset is what is large, so replicating the model would only multiply memory use.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A team is configuring how a SageMaker training job reads its dataset from Amazon S3. Which statements about the three input modes are correct?
options: Pipe streams objects through a FIFO pipe and shuffles them again on every epoch
File is the default and copies the whole dataset to the instance volume before training starts
FastFile accepts an augmented manifest as readily as a plain prefix
FastFile identifies the objects but downloads nothing, streaming from S3 on demand
Training data and checkpoints must be stored in the same Region as the job
Pipe downloads the full dataset to local disk before the first training step runs
questions.explanation: AWS documents three input modes: File as the default that copies everything to the instance first, FastFile which identifies objects and streams them with prefix-only input, and Pipe which streams through a FIFO pipe with per-epoch shuffling, and it requires data and checkpoints to sit in the job's Region. FastFile cannot read an augmented manifest, and Pipe never stages the whole dataset locally.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Place the states of a SageMaker training job in the order they occur for a job that runs to a successful finish.
options: Training, where the algorithm runs on the downloaded data
Starting, where the job request is accepted and the training container is prepared
Uploading, where the final model artifacts are written to Amazon S3
Downloading, where the channel data is pulled onto the training instances
Deployment, where the finished model is served from a real-time endpoint
questions.explanation: AWS documents the sequence Starting, Downloading, Training and Uploading, after which the job reaches a final status such as Completed. Serving the trained model happens after the job finishes in a separate deployment step, so it is not one of the job's own states.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A training job is running on Managed Spot Training with checkpointing enabled when AWS reclaims the capacity. Place the steps that follow in the order they occur.
options: Training resumes from the checkpoint in /opt/ml/checkpoints instead of step zero
AWS reclaims the instance while the job is in the Training state
The job returns to Starting and the channel data is downloaded again
SageMaker sends SIGTERM and waits 120 seconds so checkpoint code can flush
The job restarts its training loop from the first batch with no checkpoint
questions.explanation: On a spot interruption the job is interrupted during Training, receives SIGTERM with a 120-second window to flush, then cycles back through Starting and Downloading before Training resumes from /opt/ml/checkpoints. Restarting from the first batch is what happens when no checkpoint is configured, which is the outcome the checkpoint setup prevents.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A fine-tuning job's model trains comfortably on one GPU, but the dataset is so large that a single instance would run for weeks and the team needs throughput. Which strategy fits?
options: Data parallelism: each GPU holds a full replica, sees a different batch, and gradients synchronize after each step
Model parallelism: partition the weights across GPUs until each device owns a slice
Keep the job on one GPU and raise the batch size until the data fits in memory
Run separate single-GPU jobs over dataset shards with no gradient exchange
questions.explanation: When the model fits on one GPU and the dataset is enormous, the documented answer is data parallelism: a full replica per GPU with different batches and AllReduce gradient synchronization, which the SageMaker Distributed Data Parallel library implements for AWS networks. Model parallelism is the mirror case where the weights do not fit on one device, a larger batch does not add devices, and separate jobs never share what they learn.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A six-hour built-in algorithm job runs on Managed Spot Training without checkpointing, so MaxRuntimeInSeconds is 21,600. Which configuration matches AWS's documented wait rule?
options: Set MaxWaitTimeInSeconds above 21,600 so Spot capacity can be awaited for the full run
Set MaxWaitTimeInSeconds equal to the 120-second graceful-shutdown window
Expect the wait to be capped at 3,600 seconds, so add checkpointing or run On-Demand
Leave MaxWaitTimeInSeconds unset, because non-checkpointing jobs ignore the wait entirely
questions.explanation: Without checkpointing an interrupted job would restart from zero, so AWS caps MaxWaitTimeInSeconds at 3,600 seconds for built-in and Marketplace algorithms that cannot checkpoint, and a 21,600-second runtime cannot wait that long on Spot. That leaves two documented paths: add checkpointing, where no cap applies and AWS's own demo waited 48 hours, or run On-Demand. The 120 seconds is the SIGTERM window that lets checkpoint code flush, and the wait setting is required for Spot rather than ignorable.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A team is considering reinforcement fine-tuning on Amazon Bedrock for a reward-scored task. Which set matches the guardrails AWS publishes for the feature?
options: Any dataset size is accepted as long as a reward model is trained before the job
At least 500 records, at most 66 percent of prompts unlabeled, and a 95 percent minimum gain
Exactly 20,000 prompts always, at least 100 human rankings per prompt, and no held-out set
At least 100 records, at most 20,000 prompts for Nova models, and skip it when baseline reward already exceeds 95 percent
questions.explanation: AWS documents three guardrails on reinforcement fine-tuning: a minimum of 100 records, a maximum of 20,000 prompts for Nova models, and explicit advice to skip the feature when the baseline reward already exceeds 95 percent, because there is little left to gain. The 66 percent figure is the average accuracy gain AWS claims for the feature, not a dataset ratio, and records rather than rankings per prompt are the stated minimum.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: A team is evaluating model distillation as a way to cut the cost of a fixed, high-volume task. Which statements about distillation on AWS are correct?
options: Human reviewers must rank teacher and student outputs before training can start
A teacher model generates the training data that a smaller student model learns from
AWS claims the trained student can be up to 500 percent faster and 75 percent cheaper
AWS's published claim keeps the student's accuracy loss under 2 percent
The student is produced without any training run, straight from the teacher's weights
Distillation is the first step AWS recommends when answers must cite new documents
questions.explanation: Distillation trains a smaller student on outputs the teacher model produces, and AWS claims a student that is up to 500 percent faster and 75 percent cheaper with less than 2 percent accuracy loss; those are AWS's published claims, reproduced as directions rather than guarantees. Ranking human preferences describes reinforcement learning from human feedback, the student is trained rather than copied from the teacher's weights, and the customization ladder puts retrieval ahead of distillation for document-grounded answers.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 - Describe the training and fine-tuning process for FMs
questions.question: Place the checks AWS's decision path performs when a team picks how training data reaches the job, in the order the path evaluates them.
options: Choose File mode when the total sits under the 50 to 100 GB threshold
Choose Pipe mode when the data is huge, local disk is the bottleneck, and per-epoch shuffling is wanted
Compare the total dataset size with the 50 to 100 GB threshold first
Choose FastFile when individual objects exceed 50 MB and streaming should start at once
Choose Amazon FSx for Lustre when the shape is many small files with random reads
Place the bucket in a different Region than the training job to shorten transfers
questions.explanation: AWS's threshold path starts with size: under 50 to 100 GB means File mode, the default that downloads before training. It then checks shape, where many small files or random reads go to Amazon FSx for Lustre, then object size, where individual objects above 50 MB stream with FastFile, and what remains uses Pipe with FIFO streaming and per-epoch shuffling. The dataset must live in the same Region as the job, so a cross-Region bucket is never the answer.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: An evaluation engineer holds a set of human-written reference summaries and wants an automatic metric that rewards covering the content those references contain. Which metric fits?
options: BLEU, which scores n-gram precision against human reference translations
BERTScore, which compares embedding vectors of the candidate and the reference
ROUGE, which measures n-gram overlap with the reference summaries
Perplexity, which measures how surprising the model finds the text
questions.explanation: ROUGE compares generated summaries with references, and its recall-oriented variants reward covering reference content, which is the stated goal. BLEU is precision-oriented and built for translation, BERTScore measures semantic similarity, and perplexity measures model confidence.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A customer support leader is measuring whether a generative AI assistant meets the business objective of resolving customer issues without agent involvement. Which metric best reflects that objective?
options: The fluency score produced by an automatic readability check
The task completion rate, meaning the share of conversations that reach a resolution
The average number of tokens consumed per conversation
The model's score on a general knowledge benchmark
questions.explanation: Task completion rate is a business alignment metric that measures whether users actually finish what they came to do, which is the objective stated here. Fluency and benchmark scores describe model behavior, and token count measures cost rather than outcome.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A team is planning how to evaluate a generative AI application before it goes to production. Which of these are sound elements of the evaluation plan?
options: Include human review for subjective criteria such as tone, brand voice, and style
Evaluate only on the prompts used during development, since those are already understood
Use a benchmark dataset of representative prompts that the team has not tuned against
Rely on a single automated metric as proof that the application is ready to launch
Track business measures such as task completion rate and cost per interaction alongside model quality metrics
Skip evaluation when temperature is set to 0, because outputs are then deterministic
questions.explanation: Human review for subjective criteria, an untuned benchmark set, and business measures alongside quality metrics are all documented evaluation practices. A development-only prompt set, a single metric, and determinism at temperature 0 each leave major failure modes unmeasured.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Match each evaluation metric to the purpose it serves.
options: Embeds the candidate and reference text and scores the similarity of their vectors
Has a second model score outputs against a written rubric for traits such as correctness, completeness, and tone
Measures n-gram precision against human reference translations and penalizes outputs that are too short
Measures n-gram overlap with reference summaries, rewarding coverage of the content they contain
questions.explanation: ROUGE measures n-gram overlap against reference summaries, BLEU measures n-gram precision against reference translations with a brevity penalty, BERTScore compares embeddings for semantic similarity, and LLM-as-a-judge has a second model apply a rubric at scale.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A model scores 93 percent on a widely used public benchmark but performs poorly on the company's own tasks. The provider later confirms that the benchmark questions were part of the model's pre-training corpus. Which evaluation problem does this describe?
options: Benchmark contamination, because the evaluation questions were present during pre-training
Class imbalance, because one label dominates the evaluation set
Underfitting, because the model has not seen enough task data
Prompt drift, because the benchmark prompts changed between runs
questions.explanation: Benchmark contamination inflates scores when evaluation items appeared in training data, so the result does not predict performance on unseen work.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: An assistant scores 88 percent overall on the evaluation set, but the same results show that 40 percent of requests in one language are judged incorrect. Leadership is about to approve launch based on the aggregate score. What should the evaluation team recommend?
options: Approve launch, because the aggregate score is above the target
Remove the failing language from the evaluation set and re-run
Report metrics by segment and set an acceptance threshold for each segment
Raise the temperature and re-run until the failures disappear
questions.explanation: Aggregate scores can hide large segment failures. Slice-level metrics and per-segment thresholds expose them before launch.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Match each retrieval-augmented generation evaluation metric to what it measures.
options: Whether citations point to passages that support the claim
Whether retrieved chunks are relevant to the question
Whether the answer stays consistent with retrieved chunks
Whether retrieval found all the reference passages needed
questions.explanation: Context relevance and coverage judge retrieval precision and recall, while faithfulness and citation precision judge whether the generated answer and its citations are supported by the retrieved text.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A medical publisher is judging whether generated drug summaries read with clinical nuance and the right tone. It has no set of reference summaries to compare against and needs experienced editors in the loop. Which evaluation approach fits?
options: A benchmark leaderboard comparison against other publishers
Automatic evaluation against stored ground truth responses
ROUGE scoring against a single written summary
Human-in-the-loop evaluation with the publisher's clinical reviewers
questions.explanation: Human-in-the-loop evaluation is the right fit when reference answers do not exist and subjective editorial judgment is required.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A team wants a repeatable ranking of four candidate models on question answering before any human review is scheduled. Which evaluation method should it run first?
options: A benchmark dataset with known answers re-run for every candidate
Anecdotal spot checks on whatever questions the team recalls
A single review panel that picks a winner by feel
The training loss reported by each model provider
questions.explanation: Benchmark datasets give a consistent, repeatable ranking across candidates before expensive human review.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: An evaluation dataset holds 5,000 free-form answers with no reference responses, and the team wants written justifications for each score. Which approach delivers that?
options: An automatic programmatic evaluation against stored correct answers
An LLM-as-a-judge evaluation job using a judge model
A public leaderboard comparison of the same model family
An AWS-managed human review that runs for several weeks
questions.explanation: LLM-as-a-judge scores free-form output without reference answers and returns an explanation for each judgment.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A team wants its continuous delivery pipeline to reject prompt changes that lower accuracy, without waiting on reviewers. Which Bedrock evaluation type should the pipeline run?
options: A human-in-the-loop evaluation of the production application
An LLM-as-a-judge evaluation scored on a brand voice rubric
A public benchmark comparison of the underlying model
An automatic (programmatic) Bedrock evaluation job over the stored dataset
questions.explanation: Automatic (programmatic) evaluation compares responses to stored ground truth and runs unattended, which suits a pipeline gate.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A RAG evaluation shows retrieved chunks are relevant to each question and cover the needed facts, yet generated answers still include claims not present in those chunks. Where should the team act first?
options: In retrieval, by changing chunking, top-k, and metadata filters
In generation, by tightening the prompt template or changing the generator model
In ingestion, by re-parsing the source documents
In evaluation, by rewriting the prompts in the evaluation dataset
questions.explanation: Context relevance and coverage passing with low faithfulness isolates the problem to generation rather than retrieval.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: During evaluation, a model returns correct answers, but a slight rewording of the prompt flips it to a confident wrong answer. Which metric should the team use to expose this instability?
options: Toxicity, since harmful output is the likely symptom
Citation precision, since the answer cites no sources
Robustness, since it tests consistency under input variation
Completeness, since the answer omits required detail
questions.explanation: Robustness measures how stable a model's responses stay across small variations of the same input.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A team notices the same model both generates and grades its own responses, and the grades look optimistic. What is the recommended correction?
options: Use an evaluator model from a different model family than the generator
Disable the trace logs collected during evaluation
Raise the generator's temperature during evaluation
Grade only the answers that include cited sources
questions.explanation: Using an evaluator from a different model family reduces self-preference bias in the scores.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: The team is selecting automatic text metrics for a summarization pipeline. Which statements about these metrics are accurate? (Choose three.)
options: ROUGE is recall oriented and measures overlap with reference summaries
BLEU scores paraphrases highly even when few words match the reference
BERTScore compares contextual token embeddings rather than exact matches
ROUGE can be computed without any reference text
BLEU is precision oriented and was developed for machine translation output
BERTScore uses the generator's own confidence as its similarity signal
questions.explanation: ROUGE leans recall, BLEU leans precision and originated in machine translation, and BERTScore compares embeddings instead of exact tokens.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: An application combines a knowledge base, tool calls, and a fixed four-step workflow. Which evaluations should the team run to test it? (Choose three.)
options: Run a retrieve-only evaluation so knowledge base quality is scored before generation
Publish a public benchmark score as proof the application works end to end
Execute a fixed set of end-to-end scenarios and score whether each run reached the correct outcome
Score the workflow with ROUGE against one hand-written reference answer
Inspect the recorded steps to confirm the expected tools were called in a valid order
Skip retrieval checks because generation quality already covers them
questions.explanation: Separating retrieval from generation isolates failures, and scenario plus trace testing covers tool use and multi-step orchestration.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Put the steps of running a Bedrock Model Evaluation job in order.
options: Read the evaluation report written to Amazon S3 and the console
Prepare the prompt dataset in Amazon S3, with reference responses where needed
Choose the evaluation mode and the metrics that mode supports
Update the model, prompt or retrieval settings and start a new job
Run the job and let the selected scorer score each response
questions.explanation: The job flows from data preparation to mode selection, execution, report review, and then iteration on the configuration.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Put the steps of measuring whether an AI application delivers business value in order.
options: Choose an alignment metric such as cost per interaction or user satisfaction
Compare the post-launch results with the target and decide whether to iterate
Define the business outcome the application is supposed to improve
Collect the metric from live usage after launch
Capture a baseline with the existing process before launch
questions.explanation: Business value measurement starts from the outcome, picks a metric, records a baseline, collects live data, then compares results.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Put the steps of diagnosing weak RAG answers in order.
options: Re-run the same evaluation set to confirm the effect of the change
Run a RAG evaluation over a fixed set of representative questions
Only after retrieval looks healthy, adjust the prompt or change the generator
Read the retrieval metrics, context relevance and context coverage
If retrieval is weak, fix chunking, top-k, filters or the embedding model
questions.explanation: Diagnosis runs measurement first, then retrieval fixes with verification, and only then changes to generation.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Match each leadership question with the measurement that best answers it.
prompts: Did the assistant make support agents more productive?
Are users happy with the help they received?
Can the business afford to serve every interaction?
Do users come back and keep using the assistant?
options: Post-interaction satisfaction rating
Repeat usage rate over time
Agent handling time with and without the assistant
Total AI spend divided by number of interactions
questions.explanation: Productivity maps to handling time, happiness to satisfaction ratings, affordability to cost per interaction, and retention to repeat usage.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Match each evaluation method with its main limitation.
prompts: Automatic reference metrics such as ROUGE
options: Rewards surface word overlap and needs a reference answer
Scales cheaply but inherits the judge model's blind spots
Slow and expensive; does not scale with traffic
Measures somebody else's data, not your workload
questions.explanation: Each method trades cost against validity: human review is slow, benchmarks are off-workload, ROUGE is shallow, and judges are biased.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A team runs a fully programmatic evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock over a curated dataset, with no human reviewers and no LLM judge. Which set lists the three metric families AWS provides for this mode on text?
options: Accuracy, robustness and toxicity
BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore
Faithfulness, answer relevance and context relevance
Latency, cost and throughput
questions.explanation: Bedrock's automatic evaluation mode scores accuracy, robustness and toxicity from a curated dataset with no human involvement. The other sets describe text-overlap metrics, retrieval metrics scored by a judge, and operational measures rather than this mode's built-in families.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Two candidate prompts score 78 and 79 percent on a 50-example evaluation set, and the team wants to ship the higher one. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: Ship the higher-scoring prompt because the ranking is already repeatable
Compare the two prompts on the training examples instead
Treat the gap as inconclusive and enlarge or repeat the evaluation before choosing
Average the two scores and release both prompts to users
questions.explanation: On a set this small a one-point gap sits inside the noise, so the honest reading is that the candidates are tied until the set grows or the run is repeated. Shipping on that difference, or re-testing on training data, would measure the wrong thing.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Place the steps of building an evaluation dataset for a generative AI application in the order they occur.
options: Freeze and version the set before any model comparison begins
Have subject-matter experts write the reference answers for those prompts
Retrain the model on the evaluation examples
Split the set into a development portion and a held-out portion
Sample production-like prompts that cover the cases the application will actually face
Agree the scoring rubric and the metric set the team will use
questions.explanation: The set is built from representative prompts, then reference answers, then the rubric, then split, and finally frozen so comparisons stay stable. Training on evaluation examples would destroy the purpose of the set.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A team runs an automatic evaluation job to measure harmful language and wants to use AWS's built-in data instead of uploading its own. Which built-in dataset is designed for the toxicity metric?
options: Real Toxicity
Gigaword
BoolQ
WikiText-2
questions.explanation: Real Toxicity is the built-in dataset of prompts designed to elicit toxic responses, which is what the toxicity metric scores. Gigaword serves summarization, BoolQ serves question answering and WikiText-2 serves general robustness checks, so none of them is the dataset built for harmful-language scoring.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A RAG evaluation comes back showing that every generated answer contradicts the passages retrieved for its question. How is citation coverage reported for those responses?
options: As zero, because none of the passages that should be cited were cited
As a perfect score, because unsupported answers need no citations
As an average of the citation precision scores for the same responses
As not applicable, because the answer is not grounded in the retrieved text
questions.explanation: AWS documents citation coverage as not applicable when a response is entirely unfaithful, because there is no supported claim for the metric to measure. Reporting zero would claim the metric ran and failed, a perfect score would reward unsupported output, and citation precision is a separate metric over the citations that were made.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: An evaluation team wants an LLM-as-a-judge job to score a house-style rule that AWS does not ship as a built-in metric, alongside the standard correctness checks. What does that job support?
options: Only the fixed built-in set, so the house-style rule has to be scored by hand
Custom metrics written by the team, run alongside the built-in judge metrics
Custom criteria in human evaluation only, never inside a judge job
One metric per job, so a second job is required for the house-style rule
questions.explanation: AWS lists the judge's built-in metrics such as correctness, completeness, harmfulness, refusal and tone, and allows custom metrics alongside them, so a team-specific rule can be scored in the same job. Judge jobs do accept custom metrics, human evaluation is a different mode rather than the only place customization exists, and a job is not limited to a single metric.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A vendor comparison produces candidate answers from models that run outside Amazon Bedrock, and the team wants Bedrock to score them with written explanations. Which evaluation capability makes that possible?
options: Automatic programmatic scoring, which regenerates responses inside the job
A rule that refuses responses unless the same provider produced them
Bring-your-own-response scoring, where the judge grades externally produced answers
A public benchmark ranking, which cannot include externally produced answers
questions.explanation: LLM-as-a-judge in Amazon Bedrock accepts bring-your-own responses, so outputs from any model, including ones not hosted on Bedrock, are scored with explanations. Programmatic scoring compares responses against stored ground truth rather than regenerating them, and AWS explicitly built this path so the evaluation provider does not have to match the model under test.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A RAG evaluation reports weak scores on one metric even though the retrieved passages suit the question and the answer stays consistent with them, yet the answer never addresses what the user asked. Which metric is failing?
options: Context relevance, which judges whether the retrieved text suits the question
Faithfulness, which judges whether the reply stays inside the retrieved text
Answer relevance, which judges whether the reply tackles what the user asked
Citation precision, which judges whether cited passages back the claims
questions.explanation: Answer relevance measures whether the response addresses the question, and it can fail even when retrieval quality and grounding are both fine. Context relevance and citation precision judge the retrieval side and faithfulness judges grounding, so those three would score well in this scenario.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A team configures a human-based evaluation job for responses whose quality depends on tone and brand voice. Which statements about that mode are correct?
options: Scoring is fully programmatic, so no reviewer ever sees a response
Prompts and reference responses are read from Amazon S3
It is the cheapest option for scoring very large volumes of responses
Reviewers can be the team's own employees or an AWS-managed team
The report is written to Amazon S3 and surfaced through the work-team portal
The team defines its own criteria, such as relevance, style and brand voice
questions.explanation: AWS documents human evaluation staffed by either the team's own reviewers or an AWS-managed team, with custom criteria such as relevance, style and brand voice, inputs read from Amazon S3, and a report delivered to Amazon S3 and the work-team portal. It is a human workflow rather than a programmatic one, and it is the slow, expensive path that a judge model is meant to replace when volume grows.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Match each built-in task type of an automatic evaluation job to the data shape it expects.
prompts: Free-form prompts with no fixed answer to compare against
Prompts paired with reference summaries for scoring
Prompts with a known correct answer to check
Labeled examples that sort each input into a category
options: Text classification
Question answering
General generation
Summarization
questions.explanation: AWS's automatic task types are general generation, summarization, question answering and text classification, and each expects a different dataset shape: free-form prompts, prompts with reference summaries, prompts with known answers, or labeled examples. Choosing the wrong type scores a dataset against a rubric it was never built for.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A team wants to evaluate its abstractive summarizer with an AWS built-in evaluation dataset that already carries reference summaries. Which built-in fits?
options: NaturalQuestions
TriviaQA
Gigaword
BOLD
questions.explanation: Gigaword pairs news articles with their headlines, so it ships the reference summaries that an overlap metric such as ROUGE needs, and AWS lists it under text summarization alongside the Government Report Dataset. NaturalQuestions and TriviaQA are question-answering datasets scored with exact match and F1 over words, and BOLD belongs to open-ended generation checks rather than summarization.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: A team plans to score 2,000 generations with an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation job. Which statements about that mode are correct?
options: AWS claims the judge mode delivers up to 98 percent cost savings compared with human review
Safety scoring in the judge covers harmfulness, stereotyping and refusal
User-experience scoring covers helpfulness, coherence and relevance
The judge must come from the same model family as the generator for the scores to compare
A judge job can only score responses that have stored reference answers
Human review becomes unnecessary once a judge job is configured
questions.explanation: AWS publishes up to 98 percent cost savings for LLM-as-a-judge over human review, and the judge's scoring families include safety, harmfulness, stereotyping and refusal, and user experience, helpfulness, coherence and relevance. AWS's best practice is the opposite of the same-family claim: use an evaluator from a different family so shared blind spots do not cancel out, the judge scores without requiring stored references, and human sign-off is layered on rather than replaced.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Place the steps of a layered evaluation that combines an LLM-as-a-judge run with human review, in the order the team runs them.
options: Humans review the sampled tasks and record the authoritative judgments
An evaluator model from a different family scores every generation
Release the application once judge coverage and human sign-off both pass
Select a sample of tasks for human review from the scored set
Retrain the generator on every task the judge marked down
questions.explanation: AWS's layered pattern scores everything with the judge first, at scale and from a different model family than the generator, then selects a sample of tasks for human review, has humans record the authoritative judgments on that sample, and gates the release on both. Retraining on judge failures is not part of the evaluation workflow, and human review is layered in for authority rather than replaced by the judge.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 - Describe methods to evaluate FM performance
questions.question: Match each programmatic evaluation metric to how AWS says its score should be read.
prompts: Accuracy on a labeled evaluation set
options: Lower values mean spaces, casing and typos move the score less
Closer to 0 means cleaner output, scored with Detoxify
0 to 1, with higher values meaning more predictions match the labels
questions.explanation: The three programmatic metrics are read differently: accuracy is a 0 to 1 share of predictions matching ground truth where higher is better, robustness is inverted so a lower value means the model tolerates whitespace, casing and typo variations, and toxicity runs Detoxify where closer to 0 is cleaner. Treating higher as always better would misreport two of the three families that a fully programmatic evaluation job returns.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 - Explain the development of AI systems that are responsible
questions.question: A consumer-lending team notices that its approval model rejects applicants from one demographic group at roughly twice the rate of every other group, even though overall accuracy looks acceptable. Which analysis should the team perform first?
options: Compare approval and error rates across demographic subgroups to size the disparity
Train the model for more epochs so it sees every example more often
Average the predictions of several models to smooth out individual decisions
Raise the decision threshold so that fewer applicants are approved overall
questions.explanation: Subgroup analysis is the documented way to expose bias that an aggregate metric hides, because it measures how outcomes differ between demographic groups. More epochs, ensembling and threshold changes may move the numbers but neither detect nor explain the disparity.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 - Explain the development of AI systems that are responsible
questions.question: A marketing group generates product illustrations with a diffusion model and publishes them in advertising campaigns. Which risk should the legal team review before launch?
options: The model may overfit its training data and lose accuracy on unseen inputs
The generated images may substantially reproduce protected works, creating exposure to intellectual property infringement claims
The model may suffer from high variance that makes response latency unpredictable
The inference endpoint may exceed its provisioned throughput and be throttled
questions.explanation: Intellectual property infringement claims, alongside biased outputs and loss of customer trust, are the legal risks the responsible-AI objectives attach to generative AI. The other choices describe model quality or capacity issues rather than legal exposure.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 - Explain the development of AI systems that are responsible
questions.question: A team plans to score how truthful and trustworthy a new assistant is, using a reference dataset that a vendor assembled. What should the team establish first?
options: A larger model that can rewrite the reference answers automatically before scoring
A plan to drop the reference dataset and rely on unsupervised metrics instead
A measured audit of a sample of the reference labels performed by human reviewers
A higher sampling temperature so the assistant produces more varied answers
questions.explanation: Label quality analysis through human audits of a sampled set is how a team decides whether reference labels can be trusted as evidence of truthfulness. Rewriting labels with a model, discarding the dataset and changing sampling temperature do not validate the labels themselves.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 - Explain the development of AI systems that are responsible
questions.question: A team is preparing the training and evaluation data for a customer-service model that must serve a global audience. Which practices belong in a responsible dataset plan?
options: Represent the demographic groups the system will serve with inclusive, diverse examples
Balance the label distribution so that one outcome does not dominate the dataset
Draw from curated sources whose origin and usage rights are documented for each record
Duplicate majority-class rows until every class has an identical row count
Audit a sample of the labels with human reviewers before training begins
Remove every record belonging to the smallest demographic group to avoid unequal treatment
questions.explanation: Inclusivity, diversity, curated and documented sources, balanced datasets and label quality are the dataset characteristics the responsible-AI objectives name. Duplicating majority rows adds no new coverage, and deleting a small group removes exactly the representation the plan is meant to protect.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 - Explain the development of AI systems that are responsible
questions.question: Match each responsible-AI feature to the definition it describes.
options: The system works for people across different languages, cultures and abilities
Outputs are truthful and faithful to the source material they are based on
Outcomes do not differ unfairly between demographic groups
The system avoids producing content that could cause harm or endanger users
Performance stays stable when inputs are noisy, adversarial or slightly changed
questions.explanation: Fairness concerns equal treatment across groups, robustness concerns stability under perturbation, veracity concerns truthfulness against sources, safety concerns avoiding harm, and inclusivity concerns serving a diverse population. Each definition therefore pairs with exactly one of the five features.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 - Explain the development of AI systems that are responsible
questions.question: A hiring model is trained on the records of people the company hired in the past. Everyone who applied but was rejected is absent from the data. Which data problem should the team address first?
options: Measurement bias, because interviewers score candidates on different scales
Label bias, because reviewers disagree about what a good hire looks like
Data drift, because the job market changes after deployment
Selection bias, because the sample contains only applicants who were hired
questions.explanation: Selection bias arises when the training sample represents only one outcome of the population, here the applicants who were hired. The model never learns from rejected applicants.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 - Explain the development of AI systems that are responsible
questions.question: A hospital pilots a patient-facing symptom checker. Which practices belong in a responsible development plan before launch?
options: Have clinicians review a sample of outputs and define escalation for high-risk cases
Red-team the assistant with adversarial and edge-case prompts before launch
Document the intended use, known limitations and the populations the evaluation covered
Measure performance separately for the demographic groups the system will serve
Remove all disclaimers so patients place more trust in the tool
Assume the vendor's safety training covers every clinical risk
questions.explanation: Responsible pilots combine human oversight for high-risk cases, adversarial testing, documented limitations and subgroup evaluation. Disclaimers and vendor assurances do not replace those controls.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 - Explain the development of AI systems that are responsible
questions.question: Match each type of bias to the situation that demonstrates it.
options: Annotators apply inconsistent or subjective judgments
A group is left out of the dataset entirely
Training rows cover only customers who completed a purchase
A feature is recorded differently across sites or devices
Analysts look only for evidence that supports their hypothesis
questions.explanation: Selection bias narrows the sample to one outcome, measurement bias records a feature inconsistently, label bias comes from subjective annotation, confirmation bias skews analysis, and exclusion bias omits a group.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 - Explain the development of AI systems that are responsible
questions.question: A regulated lending process requires that a compliance officer can pause the decisioning model and override any individual outcome at any moment. Which responsible AI dimension does this requirement address?
options: Veracity, meaning factual correctness of the model's outputs
Controllability, meaning mechanisms to monitor and steer system behavior
Inclusivity, meaning coverage of the intended user groups
Governance, meaning the provider's supply-chain best practices
